segments.text: RealPeep is a research prototype for anonymous proof of capture. It asks whether you can prove a video came from real hardware, in a real place, without revealing which device.
The demo runs entirely in the browser. No server, no upload. Up top are the main demo and an advanced hash-chain view.
I enter a PIN, record a short clip, and stop. The certificate is built from a real frame hash chain and a simulated mesh witness. The hashing is real. The mesh here is a simulation.
Now the zero-knowledge pipeline. With the normal passphrase, the proof verifies, and the notary sees a clear result. No coercion flag.
With the duress passphrase, the captor still sees a verified proof. Only the notary sees the duress signal. That property is the point of the next slice.

The current demo uses a four-bit marker, so it is not a security result. The audit documents the eight-bit Python marker, the reusable nonce, and the missing transcript binding. The next slice replaces them.
The circuit is nineteen thousand constraints. The suite has two hundred ninety-two tests. The next milestone is on-device proving on a Pixel 8a, with a Moto G7 Power as the low-end floor.
The code, the audit, and the first failing tests are public. The next task is a transcript-bound duress tag, then on-device proving.
